sources.news_title: Federal Prosecutors Charge ICE Officer Over Alleged False Statements
sources.text:
Federal prosecutors have charged U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Christian Castro with allegedly lying to investigators about the January shooting of Venezuelan national Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis during an immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis.
Authorities previously dropped charges against Sosa-Celis and another man after video evidence appeared to contradict claims that they attacked an officer with a broom handle and snow shovel. The investigation subsequently shifted toward the conduct of law enforcement officers involved in the encounter.
The federal charges follow an investigation into whether initial reports of the encounter were fabricated. The case comes as public scrutiny of the Trump administration’s immigration policies continues, with a recent AP-NORC poll finding that 39% of U.S. adults approve of its handling of immigration, down from 49% earlier this year.

sources.news_title: Federal prosecutors charge TX ICE officer MN failed to extradite
sources.text:
Federal prosecutors have reportedly charged an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent accused of shooting a Venezuelan immigrant during the Trump administration’s January immigration crackdown in Minnesota.
Christian Castro, who is accused of shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the thigh during the Jan. 14 incident, has reportedly been charged with making false statements to federal investigators, according to the Associated Press. The charges remain under seal.
Recommended Stories
Castro is separately facing state charges in Minnesota of four counts of second-degree assault with a dangerous weapon and one count of falsely reporting a crime in connection with the shooting.
The federal case comes after a prosecutor handling the matter reportedly told attorneys for Sosa-Celis and other victims earlier this week that Justice Department officials had blocked an effort to charge Castro related to federal civil rights, according to ProPublica.
Castro had been held in a Texas prison after Minnesota prosecutors charged him in connection with the shooting in May. He was released last week after Gov. Greg Abbott (R-TX) failed to sign an extradition request from Minnesota within 90 days.
Abbott refused to sign the extradition request, arguing that Castro returned to Texas for work rather than attempt to escape criminal prosecution in Minnesota.
The federal charges are the latest development in a saga that has become a bitter showdown between a red and blue state.
Under Texas law, defendants arrested on out-of-state warrants must be released after 90 days if the state has not completed the extradition process.
Abbott also pointed to the Minnesota fraud case in his reasoning. “I don’t trust [Gov. Tim Walz (D-MN)] on anything, let alone something like this,” he said as the litigation was ongoing.
Meanwhile, Minnesota officials argued that Castro should face justice for his crimes.
ICE officer extradition fight sparks rare constitutional test
“In Minnesota, we believe in equal justice under the law. That means nobody is above the law, including agents of the federal government,” Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, a Democrat, said.
Ellison sued Abbott to force an extradition, arguing that the governor’s failure to sign the document was preventing Minnesota from prosecuting Castro. But a federal judge ruled that Minnesota’s lawsuit was premature, allowing Castro to walk free on Aug. 27.

sources.news_title: ICE agent charged with lying under oath about Minnesota shooting
sources.text:
ICE agent charged with lying under oath about Minnesota shooting
Authorities say agent fired into home with people inside, lied about circumstances.
Federal prosecutors in the United States have charged an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of lying under oath to investigators regarding the shooting of a Venezuelan man during an immigration crackdown this year.
Prosecutors alleged that Christian Castro lied to federal investigators about the events that led up to him firing on 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis through the door of a Minnesota home in January.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Mother and daughter detained by ICE in hospital after car crash
- list 2 of 3US judge declines Minnesota’s effort to force Texas to extradite ICE agent
- list 3 of 3Ex-ICE agent charged over shooting is freed by Texas authorities
The Associated Press news agency and The New York Times reported the indictment, quoting a person familiar with the matter who was not authorised to discuss the investigation publicly. It was expected to be unsealed when Castro is detained.
Castro, a former Department of Homeland Security agent, also faces multiple state felony charges in Minnesota related to the nonfatal shooting, including assault with a dangerous weapon.
Authorities in the Midwestern state had sought to extradite Castro from Texas to face trial. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican and President Donald Trump loyalist, declined to cooperate with the request.
The ensuing standoff left Castro detained in Texas for 90 days before his release last week. Under Texas law, the state cannot hold the subject of an extradition order for longer than that. His whereabouts were unclear as of Thursday.
The charges mark a rare move by the Department of Justice under Trump.
Trump’s top officials have repeatedly argued that immigration agents maintain broad protections while conducting enforcement, a position rejected by many legal experts.
For example, no one has been charged in the fatal shootings by immigration agents of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January.
An Associated Press review conducted in February found about two dozen ICE employees and contractors had faced criminal charges since 2020.
An American Civil Liberties Union report released in July documented instances of violent tactics or other civil rights violations in about a third of 1,200 immigration enforcement incidents reviewed in 2025 alone.
Video evidence contradicts statement
The Trump administration distanced itself from the Castro case after video emerged contradicting the agent’s initial accounts of the confrontation.
Castro told investigators that Sosa-Celis had attacked him, which the surveillance footage showed did not happen.
Todd Lyons, then acting head of ICE, said at the time that the footage “has revealed that sworn testimony provided by two separate officers appears to have made untruthful statements”.
Castro and a fellow agent chased Alfredo Aljorna, a Venezuelan national, after a traffic stop, according to charging documents.
Aljorna fled to the home he shared with Sosa-Celis. After a brief scramble, the two men ran inside. Castro then shot through the closed door, “knowing [the home] was occupied by several people”, the documents said.
One witness said there were two children in the house when Castro opened fire. Sosa-Celis was hit in the leg.
Federal authorities have since suspended Castro and dropped all charges against Sosa-Celis and his co-defendant, who were both initially accused of forcibly assaulting an ICE officer. The other agent involved in the incident was also suspended, but has not yet been charged.
Thursday’s indictment comes after ProPublica this week reported that Department of Justice (DOJ) officials had blocked prosecutors from pursuing more serious civil rights charges against Castro, including “deprivation of rights under color of law”.
However, a source close to the investigation told the AP the active investigation could still result in civil rights charges.
The Trump administration has scaled back the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division and dismantled several Biden-era police oversight initiatives since returning to office in January 2025.
That has come as the administration has revved up its mass deportation campaign across the country.
In August, immigration agents detained 50,925 people with the Department of Homeland Security hailing it as a new record for the “highest number of illegal aliens arrested in a single month”.

sources.news_title: ICE agent charged with lying about shooting Venezuelan man during crackdown
sources.text:
ICE agent charged with lying about shooting Venezuelan man during crackdown
- Published
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent has been charged with lying about the non-fatal shooting of a Venezuelan migrant in the state of Minnesota.
Christian Castro, who is not yet in custody, faces a six-count federal indictment relating to shooting on 14 January, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS.
The Department of Homeland Security initially said he fired in self-defence after being attacked by three Venezuelan illegal migrants with a shovel and broom handle. Minnesota investigators allege Castro fired through a closed door, shooting the man in the leg.
It is rare for the current justice department to accuse a federal agent of breaking the law on the job.
- What is ICE and what powers do its agents have to use force? 
  - Published4 February
In Minnesota, Castro faces separate charges of assault and false reporting of a crime related to the shooting.
Castro was one of thousands of federal immigration officers deployed to the Midwestern state during Operation Metro Surge, which sparked fierce protests and resulted in the deaths of two US citizens at the hands of agents during confrontations.
Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna and Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, who was shot in the leg and survived, were originally charged with forcibly assaulting, resisting or impeding federal officers.
After surveillance video raised questions about the agents' version of events, federal prosecutors investigated them.
In February, ICE said two immigration agents might have made "untruthful statements" about the shooting. They were placed on administrative leave.
The charges against the migrants were dismissed, with prosecutors citing "newly discovered evidence", CBS reported.
Castro was arrested in Texas in May and detained for three months.
Minnesota's top prosecutor asked for him to be extradited to stand trial, but Texas Governor Greg Abbott said he did not approve the request because he had "serious doubts" that Castro qualified as a fugitive.
Castro was released from custody in Texas last week.
Minnesota officials have said the agent discharged his weapon through the front door of a home "knowing there were people who had just run inside".
The bullet went through the door and struck one person in the leg, making its final impact in the wall of a child's room, they said.
The BBC has approached the office of Minnesota's top prosecutor for comment.

sources.news_title: ICE Officer Charged With Lying About Minneapolis Shooting After Video Casts Doubt on Claims Venezuelan Man Attacked
sources.text:
ICE Officer Charged With Lying About Minneapolis Shooting After Video Casts Doubt on Claims Venezuelan Man Attacked
Federal charges filed against ICE officer Christian Castro for lying about a shooting incident in Minneapolis
A federal grand jury indicted an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer for lying about a shooting that wounded a Venezuelan man and left a Minneapolis neighbourhood in uproar.
The case against Christian Castro is one of the few instances in which the Department of Justice has moved to hold an ICE agent criminally accountable during President Donald Trump's mass deportation drive.
Federal prosecutors in Minnesota charged Castro, 52, with making false statements about the events preceding the 14 January 2026 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity. The indictment, handed up on 2 September, remains under seal.
Shooting Through a Closed Door
Castro was working in north Minneapolis as part of Operation Metro Surge, the Department of Homeland Security's largest-ever immigration enforcement operation, when he and another officer chased Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna to a duplex where Aljorna lived with Sosa-Celis. Prosecutors allege Castro fired through the home's closed front door.
The bullet struck Sosa-Celis in the thigh before travelling through a closet and lodging in the wall of a child's bedroom, according to Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison's office. Castro was outside and alone in the front yard when he fired, the Attorney General's office said. Homeland Security's initial account differed sharply.
The department's 15 January press release claimed Castro had been struck with shovels, brooms or other weapons, an assertion Ellison's office says is false and which remains uncorrected on the DHS website. Sosa-Celis and Aljorna were initially charged with assaulting a federal officer; both cases were dropped after surveillance video surfaced.
Video Evidence Undoes Official Account
Castro told FBI investigators that he and a fellow officer had been beaten with a snow shovel and a broom handle by the two Venezuelan men, prompting him to open fire in self-defence, according to NewsNation's source. Surveillance footage and witness statements contradicted that version, prosecutors say.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty charged Castro in state court on 18 May with four felony counts of second-degree assault with a dangerous weapon and one misdemeanour count of falsely reporting a crime.
Moriarty told reporters that Castro allegedly fired his gun 'with the intent to cause fear of immediate bodily harm or death to the four adults who were just inside the door'.
Ellison was blunt about the discrepancy between the official DHS narrative and what investigators found. 'Nobody is above the law, including ICE agents,' he said, adding that 'the State of Minnesota must hold people accountable for violating the law and for harming Minnesotans'.
The federal charge adds to that state case rather than replacing it. Castro faces six separate counts related to lying to investigators, though the indictment's contents will not be public until unsealed, a NewsNation source said. Castro is expected to be transferred into federal custody imminently.
An Extradition Fight and a Downgraded Charge
The case became entangled in an unusual interstate standoff after Castro was arrested by Texas Rangers and Homeland Security's inspector general in Cameron County on 29 May.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott refused to sign Minnesota's extradition warrant, prompting Ellison to sue him. Under Texas law, Castro had to be released if not extradited within ninety days; he walked free from a Brownsville jail on 27 August after a federal judge declined to intervene.
Ellison's office had warned that Castro, who maintains a relationship and property in Mexico, posed a flight risk given his proximity to the border.
Ellison called the episode 'not politics' and 'not a game'.
The federal charges brought this week are notably narrower than what career prosecutors initially sought.
According to internal ProPublica documents reported by Minnesota Reformer, Justice Department officials in Washington blocked prosecutors from pursuing civil rights violations against Castro, insisting instead on the single false-statements charge now reflected in the indictment.
Matthew Evans, the assistant US attorney handling the case, wrote in an email to victims' lawyers that he had objected 'in the strongest possible terms' to that decision.
ICE's then-acting director, Todd Lyons, addressed Castro's suspension when it was first announced in February. 'The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity and ethical conduct,' Lyons said. 'Violations of this sacred sworn oath will not be tolerated.'
The shooting occurred against a violent backdrop in Minneapolis, coming roughly a week after the fatal shooting of Renee Good and roughly a week and a half before the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti, both involving federal immigration agents during the same operation. No agent has yet been charged in either of those deaths.
Castro's case now heads towards a federal arraignment, with the Minnesota state charges still pending separately in Hennepin County.

sources.news_title: Federal prosecutors charge ICE officer with lying to investigators in the shooting of Venezuelan immigrant
sources.text:
An ICE officer is facing federal charges for allegedly lying to federal investigators about the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant during immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis earlier this year.
A federal grand jury on Wednesday returned an indictment charging the officer, Christian Castro, with making false statements to the FBI about the Jan. 14 shooting that left Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis with a gunshot wound in his leg, a source familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
A separate investigation into whether Castro should face a more serious civil rights charge in the shooting is ongoing, the source added.
The Associated Press first reported on Castro’s latest federal charges.
The federal charges come a week after Castro was released from jail in Texas despite an extradition warrant from Minnesota prosecutors seeking his transfer. He’s facing state charges in Minnesota accusing him of assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.
Federal authorities had initially accused Sosa-Celis and another man of beating an immigration officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel in a confrontation that preceded the shooting, but federal prosecutors dropped the charges they filed against the men after video evidence showed the ICE officers may have lied about the encounter.
Castro was arrested in May in the Minnesota case. He was held in custody in Brownsville, Texas, until his release last week after a judge and Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign his extradition warrant — citing fraud investigations involving social services programs in Minnesota, which the Trump administration used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

Mahaleris added that “details of any federal indictment are best addressed to the U.S. Department of Justice.”
The Department of Homeland Security and the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office referred any queries to the DOJ.
An attorney for Castro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As news broke of Castro’s latest indictment, a federal prosecutor working on the case against Castro was fired, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Evans had told lawyers for Sosa-Celis that DOJ officials have blocked efforts to bring the more serious civil rights charge against Castro, ProPublica reported on Wednesday.
Evans did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and his DOJ email address returned an automated reply saying he was on leave.

Federal prosecutors have charged U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro with making false statements about the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis Jan. 14, the New York Times reported Thursday, citing an unnamed person familiar with the case.
The Times reported that the indictment will be unsealed after Castro is taken into custody.
The federal charge against an ICE agent is a rare move for the administration of President Donald Trump, which still has not charged any of the agents involved in the January killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
The single charge against Castro is far less than the civil rights violations originally sought by local federal prosecutors. But officials at the Department of Justice in Washington D.C. insisted the charges be significantly downgraded, according to reporting from ProPublica.
Castro is also charged in Minnesota with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. He is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a north Minneapolis home, hitting Cesar-Solis in the leg and endangering other people in the home.
Castro accused Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan immigrant of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.
In an email obtained by ProPublica, Matthew Evans, the assistant U.S. attorney in Minnesota in charge of the case, told attorneys for Sosa-Celis and other victims that he “objected in the strongest possible terms” to his bosses’ decision not to pursue civil rights charges.
Castro was released from a Texas county jail on Aug. 27, 90 days after his arrest by Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency, pursuant to the warrant related to his Minnesota charges.
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott blocked Castro’s extradition to Minnesota, prompting a lawsuit from Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison. A federal judge in that case declined to force the extradition, paving the way for Castro’s release.

By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff and Jonathan Allen
WASHINGTON, Sept 3 (Reuters) – An immigration officer has been indicted by a federal grand jury on charges of making false statements about the shooting of a Venezuelan man in Minnesota during a deportation surge last winter, according to a source familiar with the matter on Thursday.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro was indicted on six counts of lying to investigators, the person said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the investigation. The charges will be unsealed once Castro is in custody, the person said.
The charges are an extraordinary step by a Justice Department that has refrained from alleging criminal wrongdoing by federal officers. This is the first known Justice Department prosecution of a federal immigration officer over wrongdoing in the Minneapolis operation, part of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
Castro faces state charges in Minnesota for shooting and wounding Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg on January 14, at the height of Trump’s deportation campaign in Minnesota, which drew weeks of protest.
There is an active Minnesota state arrest warrant for Castro, who spent 90 days in a Texas county jail. He was released last week after Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, said he was refusing to sign extradition papers sent by Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, a Democrat.
The state charges also include falsely reporting a crime after Castro allegedly wrongly told superiors at the Department of Homeland Security that Sosa-Celis and others attacked him with a snow shovel and broom, which was disproved by video evidence.
DHS has suspended Castro, and the person familiar with the case said a civil rights investigation is ongoing and no decision has been reached yet in that matter.
Matt Evans, a federal prosecutor who had been working on the case, was fired this week after ProPublica reported he sent an email to Sosa-Celis’ lawyers saying DOJ attorneys had stopped his efforts to bring federal charges, according to the person familiar with the case. Evans is now being investigated for obstruction of a grand jury investigation, the person said.
Castro has not publicly addressed the state charges against him since his release from the Cameron County jail last week, and he could not immediately be reached for comment on Thursday.
The Trump administration has largely defended the conduct of ICE agents, saying incorrectly that they have absolute immunity from state prosecutions.
Robin Wolpert, a lawyer for Sosa-Celis, said in a statement her client wants Castro to be held “fully accountable” with stronger civil rights charges. “Mr. Castro has been indicted for making false statements,” she said. “But he made them to cover up the fact that he shot my client through the door of an occupied house without a self-defense justification.”
The ACLU of Minnesota announced on Thursday that it will represent Sosa-Celis as he sues the Trump administration.

A federal grand jury has indicted an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer on charges of making false statements about the nonfatal shooting of a man during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota last winter, according to a person familiar with the case who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive information.

Castro, who had been previously charged in state court, was among the thousands of federal agents who flooded Minnesota over the objections of local officials. Those agents made thousands of arrests, clashed regularly with residents and shot three people during the campaign, leaving two U.S. citizens dead.
The indictment against Castro was filed under seal, and officials expect to make it public once he is in custody.
Prosecutors said Castro shot and wounded Julio C. Sosa-Celis, who is from Venezuela and who lacked legal status in the United States. The Jan. 14 shooting was followed by hours of protests and vandalism.
Top Trump administration officials initially came to Castro’s defense. A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer has been federally charged for allegedly lying to investigators about the January shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant during an immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis, according to multiple news reports.
Christian Castro, who already faces criminal charges in Minnesota in connection with the shooting, was indicted Sept. 2 by a federal grand jury on six counts of making false statements, CBS News and MS Now reported. The indictment remained under seal Sept. 3, and law enforcement officers were attempting to locate Castro, according to CBS News.
The charges stem from the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis during the Trump administration's Operation Metro Surge, a large immigration enforcement operation in Minnesota's Twin Cities region. Authorities said the bullet later lodged in a child's bedroom wall.
Castro also faces Minnesota state charges alleging he assaulted Sosa-Celis and falsely reported a crime.
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has refused to extradite Castro to Minnesota, prompting an ongoing legal fight between the two states. Castro was released from a Texas jail last week after a judge declined to order his return to Minnesota.

In the days after the shooting, the Department of Homeland Security said Castro acted in self-defense after Sosa-Celis and another man attacked him with a broomstick and shovel while trying to evade arrest. The case took another turn in February when then acting ICE Director Todd Lyons said video evidence appeared to contradict sworn testimony from Castro and another officer, according to CBS News.
"Video evidence has revealed that sworn testimony provided by two separate officers appears to have made untruthful statements," Lyons said. This is the first time the Justice Department has charged an officer for conduct that occurred on-duty during highly publicized immigration operations nationwide. Local prosecutors in Minnesota had already charged Castro with second-degree assault and making a false report earlier this year.
CNN attempted to reach a lawyer for Castro for comment.
The Justice Department is still considering whether to bring civil rights charges against Castro, one of the sources said.
Castro also faces the separate state charges in Minnesota. He was released from a Texas jail last week after the governor there declined to immediately approve his extradition to Minnesota.
Federal prosecutors initially charged 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, whom Castro shot, and another man with attacking an ICE officer with a snow shovel and broom stick. But those charges were dropped after investigators reviewed surveillance footage and other material from the incident that conflicted with Castro’s account.
Castro and a second agent were soon placed on administrative leave. Federal prosecutors told the judge overseeing the case against Sosa-Celis that the agents had made “false statements” under oath, and former ICE Director Todd Lyons said later the Justice Department was investigating the “untruthful statements.”
Prosecutors in Minnesota, who charged Castro in May, allege that he shot Sosa-Celis in the back of the leg through the door of Sosa-Celis’ apartment.
The shooting occurred after ICE officers had attempted to pull over a truck belonging to an undocumented immigrant named Joffre Barrera, the state alleged. Sosa-Celis’ cousin and DoorDash driver, Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna, was behind the wheel and drove off from the officers, they said.
According to Sosa-Celis, Aljorna ran from the truck and was tackled steps away from Sosa-Celis’ apartment by an ICE agent. Sosa-Celis called for Aljorna to get inside and, once both cousins were behind the door, a shot rang out, Sosa-Celis said.
“I closed the door and as I was locking it, I heard the shot, and that’s when I realized I had been shot in the leg,” Sosa-Celis told CNN at the time during a Facebook livestream from a hospital.
Color of law cases are often very complicated, and have historically taken months or years to bring. It took the department nearly a year to bring a civil rights case against Derek Chauvin related to George Floyd’s death, and more than two years for the department to charge Louisiana Metro Police Department officers connected to Breonna Taylor’s killing.
Earlier this week, a federal prosecutor working on the case told lawyers for Sosa-Celis and other victims that Justice Department officials blocked the push to bring a more serious civil rights charge against Castro for the shooting, ProPublica reported on Wednesday.
A person familiar with the matter told CNN a formal decision on whether to bring those civil rights charges has not been made. The prosecutor, Matthew Evans, was fired and is under investigation for alleged obstruction of a grand jury probe, according to the person.
An automatic response from Evan’s department email said he was “on leave.” CNN made multiple other attempts to reach him.
“Mr. Castro has been indicted for making false statements. But he made them to cover up the fact that he shot my client through the door of an occupied house without a self-defense justification,” Sosa-Celis’ lawyer, Robin M. Wolpert, said in a statement to CNN. “Although the evidence strongly supports civil rights charges, the federal government has grossly undercharged this case. Mr. Sosa Celis wants Mr. Castro to be held fully accountable for his crimes.”
This story has been updated with additional information.

sources.news_title: Trump DOJ charges ICE agent with lying about Minneapolis shooting
sources.text:
Federal prosecutors have charged a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with lying to investigators about a January shooting that wounded a Venezuelan man during an immigration crackdown in Minneapolis.
Christian Castro, the officer accused of shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg, faces a federal false statements charge after authorities determined video evidence contradicted initial accounts of the encounter.
The development comes amid a widening investigation that has already led prosecutors to drop charges against Sosa-Celis and follows reports of internal Justice Department (DOJ) disagreements over whether to pursue additional civil rights charges.
Newsweek has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, the DOJ and Minnesota Governor Tim Walz via email on Thursday afternoon for comment. DHS referred Newsweek to the DOJ.
Christian Castro Charges: What To Know
Castro was charged with making false statements to federal investigators after his release from jail in Texas on August 27.
He had been under arrest following charges out of Minnesota in connection with the shooting of Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis on January 14, at the height of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in the Twin Cities, and a week after U.S. citizen Renee Nicole Good was shot dead by an ICE agent.
The agent and another officer had chased another man, Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna, into a duplex apartment where the pair lived. Both had legal status at the time.
Officers initially alleged that Aljorna violently resisted arrest and that Sosa-Celis and another man allegedly tried to intervene by attacking the officer with a shovel and broom handle, per an FBI investigator's affidavit. At that point, Sosa-Celis was shot in the leg by a federal agent before fleeing into a nearby apartment. He was then detained.
Agents, including Castro, were later accused of lying under oath and were placed under investigation. Video published in April appeared to contradict the original official version of events.
In May, ICE told Newsweek that lying under oath was a serious offense and added that the U.S. Attorney's Office was actively investigating the allegations.
Tensions Over Castro's Extradition
Last week, a federal judge denied Minnesota's request to extradite Castro from Texas, where he had been held following his arrest over the state-level charges.
U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr., an appointee of President Donald Trump, ruled that Minnesota had failed to meet the legal requirements for a temporary restraining order because Governor Greg Abbott had not formally rejected the state's extradition request and was still reviewing whether Castro should be surrendered.
Minnesota, led by Democrat Tim Walz, had argued that Abbott was effectively blocking extradition by failing to sign a rendition warrant more than two months after Texas authorities arrested Castro.
Rare Federal Charges
While ICE agents have largely avoided criminal prosecution for their immigration enforcement activities, there have been some exceptions in recent years.
An Associated Press review found that at least two dozen ICE employees and contractors have faced criminal charges since 2020 in cases ranging from corruption and bribery to sexual abuse and other misconduct, highlighting concerns from some watchdogs and former officials about oversight as the agency expands.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Sam Wilson.

sources.text:
DOJ charges ICE agent with lying about Minneapolis shooting
The Department of Justice has charged U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian J. Castro with making false statements to federal investigators after a Venezuelan man was shot in Minneapolis earlier this year, according to ABC and The Associated Press sources.
Castro, 52, shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis on Jan. 14 in Minneapolis after Sosa-Celis allegedly ran from a traffic stop.
Castro was previously charged via warrant in Hennepin County; he was arrested in Texas, where a federal judge denied Minnesota’s request to compel his extradition. Last week, Castro was released from jail.
Following his release, Homeland Security suspended Castro without pay, a source with the department told 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS last week.
Background
Back in January, Homeland Security initially said three people assaulted Castro with a snow shovel and broom handles for three minutes, but video of the incident released by the City of Minneapolis contradicts that claim.
RELATED: ICE agent charged in non-fatal shooting of Venezuelan man
The video shows Sosa-Celis running toward a house on 24th Avenue North, slipping, and falling before Castro catches up. Another man is then seen dropping a snow shovel and going inside the house.
Charging documents in Hennepin County say Castro fired into the home, hitting Sosa-Celis in the leg and endangering the two kids and three adults inside the home.
Castro’s version of events, as detailed in an FBI affidavit, describes three men beating him with a shovel and a broom. Despite claiming to be outnumbered three to one and enduring the assault “for about three minutes … exhausted, alone, on the ground, and in fear of his safety,” Castro claimed he blocked most of their blows to avoid injury. A previous complaint filed in Hennepin County, citing medical records, states Castro “suffered no demonstrable trauma to his body except for an abrasion to his left hand at the base of his thumb.”
A spokesperson for ICE previously called the charges filed against Castro “unlawful and nothing more than a political stunt.”
RELATED: ICE agent charged in Minneapolis shooting released from Texas jail
Federal charges against Sosa-Celis and his roommate, Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna, were dismissed with prejudice after government prosecutors said “newly discovered evidence” clashed with the accounts of the ICE agents involved.

The Trump administration on Thursday again asked the Supreme Court to let it move ahead with restrictions on mail ballots before this year’s the midterm elections in November.
The government filed an emergency appeal asking the court to intervene after a judge in Boston handed down a new decision blocking President Trump’s executive order for two weeks.
