Follow along live.
White House website now features arcade games — 6:03 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The White House website has unveiled Arcade, a collection of five low-resolution video games that promote different aspects of the president’s agenda.
“Build the Wall” is a “Tetris” knockoff that transforms the classic game into an effort to “Protect the border from the coming horde.” In ”Rio Run,” which resembles the mobile favorite “Snake,” an icon resembling Trump runs around gathering potential border crossers.
In “Supply Line,” which looks like a condensed version of the arcade game “Tapper,” food moves along an assembly line and you must reject items that don’t meet “Make America Healthy Again” standards.
Two of the games take place over the skies of the nation’s capital. In “Flappy Bill,” an eagle carries a bill across the National Mall. In “Trump Savings Tycoon,” your goal is to collect money flying through the air to “Fill your kids’ Trump Accounts,” the administration savings plan that offers $1,000 to every child born during Trump’s term.
Missouri court blocks Trump-backed US House map and orders it to be put to a vote — 6:01 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The Missouri Supreme Court has ruled that the map cannot be used until voters first get a chance in November to uphold or reject it.
Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins had turned down a citizens’ petition seeking to put the map to a vote. But the court reversed that decision and ordered a referendum to be held.
The decision Thursday marks a rare setback for Republicans in a national redistricting battle. Republicans had hoped Missouri’s new congressional boundaries could help them win an additional seat and hold onto their slim House majority in the midterms. The ruling still could be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Virginia Democrat calls Trump’s arch a ‘monstrosity’ — 5:51 p.m.
By the Associated Press
U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, whose congressional district includes Arlington National Cemetery, said the administration has not addressed concerns about traffic, disruptions and other issues related to the proposed arch in Washington.
“This project is not even close to being ready for prime time,” said Beyer, whose parents, grandparents and sister are buried at Arlington.
He has proposed a viewshed protection act that would prohibit the arch’s construction.
“Donald Trump boasted aloud that his sole intent for building this arch is to honor himself,” Beyer said in a statement. “All of us who oppose it must stand up and redouble our efforts to stop this monstrosity.”
The Trump administration halted a Great Lakes project. Then Whitmer called Trump. — 5:35 p.m.
By the Associated Press
An unexplained Trump administration hold on construction of a state-federal project aimed at preventing invasive carp from reaching the Great Lakes was abruptly lifted this week, hours after a call to Trump by Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.
The Army Corps had halted work without explanation on the Brandon Road Interbasin Project near Joliet, Illinois, in July, leaving officials in Illinois and Michigan struggling for answers about the pause even as environmental officials warned that invasive carp were being found alarmingly close to Lake Michigan.
The Wednesday phone call was a surprising intervention by the Democratic governor, who has developed an unusual relationship with a president who was once one of her fiercest political foes. Hours after the call, the stop-work order was lifted.
The episode also underscores the top-down and relationship-driven nature of his administration, where direct phone calls and displays of deference to the president remain the best way to get things done.
Trump political adviser says Republicans will be pleased with upcoming spending — 5:17 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The president’s top outside political adviser says Republicans who have been clamoring for Trump to open his wallet and spend some of the enormous war chest he has amassed on the midterm elections will soon find relief.
“When it’s all said and done, all Republicans, at least, will be quite pleased and relieved at the support they find,” James Blair said at an Ohio energy affordability summit.
“You can watch the news for the next week or so, and I think the question will answer itself,” added Blair, the former White House deputy chief of staff, who recently left his post to run Trump’s outside political operation.
Trump’s MAGA Inc. group had more than $400 million cash in hand at the end of July, but has so far spent little.
Blair acknowledged an enthusiasm gap between Republican and Democratic voters, but predicted that gap would start to close as the president hits the campaign trail.
Former EPA officials accuse Trump administration of sitting on PFAS survey — 5:06 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The Trump administration has stalled a study that would help regulators understand which industries dump harmful forever chemicals with their wastewater, according to two former agency officials involved in its development.
Records show the first-of-its-kind survey of wastewater treatment plants was submitted to the White House for approval nearly two years ago during the Biden administration. The White House Office of Management and Budget must approve the survey, and the two ex-officials note reviews typically take around 60 days.
“This is sufficiently unusual and a very long period of time that it is worth asking the question: Is OMB just sitting on it?” said Stuart Shapiro, a former OMB staffer and now a dean at Rutgers University-New Brunswick in New Jersey.
The former officials say the survey would not only help officials understand the scope of PFAS is in the nation’s wastewater, but equip regulators with the information needed to consider new limits against the spread of the chemicals.
The Office of Management Budget did not respond to a request for comment.
Anti-abortion activists launch effort to suspend new Mass. abortion law, put repeal before voters — 5:03 p.m.
By Chris Van Buskirk, Globe Staff
Anti-abortion activists in Massachusetts filed paperwork with the state launching a bid to suspend and eventually seek the repeal of a law that makes it easier for women to receive an abortion later in pregnancy.
That move sets up a potential ballot battle in 2028, and more immediately, kick-starts a scramble to stop the law before it can even take effect.
Massachusetts Democrats have repeatedly stepped in to bolster the state’s reproductive health care laws in the years after the Supreme Court struck down the constitutional right to an abortion, including last month when Governor Maura Healey signed a measure making Massachusetts’s abortion laws among the broadest in the country.
Sam Miele, the director of the conservative group Massachusetts Family Action, said his group is behind the repeal push, motivated by what he called the “audacity of our governor” to approve the abortion law in early August.
“Maura Healey, she took a political bet, and it went too far,” Miele said Thursday.
The Supreme Court won’t step into a Michigan ballot dispute — 4:48 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The court has declined to intervene in a dispute over whether a proof-of-citizenship voting measure can appear on the November ballot in Michigan.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied an emergency appeal from supporters of a proposed constitutional amendment. The group Americans for Citizen Voting came to the high court after state officials declined to certify the proposal for the upcoming ballot.
If passed and enacted, the initiative would require the secretary of state to review government records to determine if registered voters are citizens. Voters who are flagged could be removed from the voter rolls if they do not provide proof of citizenship. Backers of the initiative turned in more than 700,000 signatures in March.
U.S. citizenship is required to vote across the country, and people must attest that they are citizens under penalty of perjury to register. Data indicates that voting by noncitizens is rare.
Administration files emergency appeal asking Supreme Court to lift new block on mail-voting restrictions — 4:34 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The Trump administration has again asked the Supreme Court to let it move ahead with restrictions on mail ballots before the November elections, even as legal wrangling over President Donald Trump’s executive order continues in lower courts.
The government filed an emergency appeal Thursday asking the court to intervene, one day before ballots begin going out for the midterm elections. The justices previously allowed the president’s plan to move ahead, but they have not decided whether it is legal.
Under Trump’s executive order, the U.S. Postal Service could refuse to deliver ballots from states that do not submit lists of eligible voters and follow a uniform envelope style.
The appeal came hours after a federal court hearing in Boston in which a Justice Department lawyer could not tell a judge whether the new system to regulate mail ballots was operational.
Washington panel hears opposition to Lafayette Square fencing plans — 4:15 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Proposals to install permanent fencing and gates around Lafayette Park in front of the White House have met with opposition. Several critics were heard Thursday at a federal planning board session.
The National Capital Planning Commission took another step toward the project, signaling it’s ready to vote on a final plan at a future meeting. The panel includes several Trump appointees and administration officials.
Several historic preservationists, legal authorities and residents of Washington, D.C, criticized the proposals. They’ve pushed back against Secret Service and administration arguments that permanent park fencing is needed to improve White House security.
“Why isn’t the existing White House fence, recently rebuilt, and the manifold other security measures in place around the White House adequate?” asked attorney Laura Follansbee with the local American Civil Liberties Union.
Commissioners accepted several versions of the proposal and accepted public comments into the record Thursday.
Trump administration says excavation work to start soon on Washington arch — 4:00 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The administration says excavation work will begin over the next two weeks on the site where it plans to build a towering, gilded arch.
Critics say the arch, which is being challenged in a lawsuit, would disrupt historic sightlines in the nation’s capital. The plan calls for erecting a 250-foot-tall memorial arch that is to stand between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery
“This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, befitting the most power Capital in the World,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X in announcing the work.
Trump administration imposes tariffs of up to 100 percent on foreign drones — 3:42 p.m.
By the Associated Press
A federal judge in Boston said on Thursday that the Trump administration appeared to rush changes to international student visas this summer and offered no rationale for the proposed revamp.
The change, which restricts the length of student visas to four years, is set to go into effect on Sept. 15. A lawsuit hoping to intervene beforehand is now in the hands of Judge F. Dennis Saylor.
A hearing in Boston unveiled the first lengthy justification of the rule from the Trump administration, which argued that the new system would strengthen the government’s purview over international student visas and serve as a necessary measure to prevent fraud. Saylor was not convinced.
Although he did not issue an immediate decision, Saylor said the government failed to provide any justification of the proposed four year cutoff and appeared to “push this through at high speed rather than taking the comments of the affected communities seriously.”
Trump administration imposes tariffs of up to 100 percent on foreign drones — 3:33 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The presidential order is intended to keep out Chinese-made drones and promote domestic manufacturing of the unmanned aircraft, which have become a popular consumer product and increasingly critical on the battlefield.
The tariffs took effect Thursday. The administration is imposing a 100% tariff on foreign drones that weigh more than 55 pounds, or those with thermal imaging capabilities, as well as certain drone parts. Smaller drones, or those weighing 55 pounds or less, face a 25% tariff.
The administration has capped the tariff at 15% for drones from countries such as South Korea, Japan and Switzerland as well as the European Union. Drones from the U.K. are levied at 10%.
Vance said he could support other Republicans for 2028 — 2:42 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The vice president, who is widely expected to seek the presidency in two years but hasn’t said if he will run, was asked if he’d support U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas or Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — two Republicans whose names have been floated as possible presidential candidates.
Vance said he encourages any Republican who cares about the country to focus on the midterm elections, not a job that is a few years away. But he added, “I could see myself supporting a whole host of people.”
He called Hegseth “a great guy” and of Cruz, he said: “Just, clearly, Ted is a very authentic and likeable guy and I’m sure he’ll do great.”
Democrats plan counter-programming at GOP’s midterm convention — 2:41 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, said he expects “robust engagement” by Democrats at the Trump confab next week in Dallas.
“Listen, the fact that these Republicans are planning a celebration in the middle of an economic crisis — where everyday Americans are drowning because of this high cost of living — is extraordinary,” Jeffries said at the Capitol.
“How many different ways can Donald Trump and Republicans communicate to the American people that they don’t give a damn about their health, safety, and economic well-being?”
He said Democrats from the House and Senate, alongside governors from various states and the Texas State Democrats, are planning events.
Vice president says the Federal Reserve should lower rates — 2:39 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Vance said at Thursday’s White House briefing that inflation figures show the Federal Reserve should cut its benchmark interest rates.
“Our view, and this has been a consistent message from the president and the rest of the administration on down, is that we believe that the Fed should be lowering interest rates,” Vance said. “We feel quite confident that if you look at the inflation numbers, if you look at the CPI numbers, that it’s proper and responsible for the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates.”
Fed officials, including the chair picked by Trump, Kevin Warsh, have said inflation is running above the central bank’s 2% target. That’s a sign that the Fed should either hold its rates or hike them in order to put downward pressure on inflation.
The consumer price index rose 3.4% in July over the past 12 months.
Vance says the Iran conflict is not a war — 2:30 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Vance says the ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran is not a war, two days after the U.S. wrapped up its latest round of strikes.
“I wouldn’t call it a war right now,” Vance said after a journalist used the term. “There is no active shooting.”
“Major combat operations” lasted only about six weeks, during which much of Iran’s military capabilities were destroyed, he claimed.
But he says Iran keeps firing at ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and that the U.S. must protect global shipping.
Vance defends friendship with Tucker Carlson even as commentator beefs with Trump — 2:27 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Carlson, a conservative commentator, has been deeply critical of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. The president, for his part, has lashed back at his one-time ally.
Vance says he has deep disagreements with Carlson, but they’re still friends.
“Everybody knows that Tucker Carlson and I are friends, and I think it’s very obvious that Tucker has said some things that I disagree with,” Vance said.
He added, “I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them.”
Vance says the US is investigating report of airstrike hitting an Iranian wedding — 2:26 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The vice president said he was briefed on the reported attack and said “we’re investigating it very fully.”
Iranian state media reported that four people were killed when a U.S. missile hit a home where dozens of people were gathered to celebrate a wedding.
Vance said the U.S. never targets civilians in combat, but added that “sometimes things happen.”
“We’re investigating it because obviously we care, we want to know,” Vance said. “When our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them.”
U.S. Central Command spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins previously said the U.S. military was looking into the reports.
Vance mocks the prospect of seeing Biden at the upcoming 9/11 memorial — 2:24 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The vice president was asked about his expected appearance next week in New York at a memorial to mark 25 years since the 9/11 attacks. He said he was “looking forward to it” and called it “an amazing honor.”
Vance then recalled the great sense of national unity in the wake of the 2001 attacks, adding, “that’s something that we should really try every single day to get back to, and if even just for a day, even if just for a few hours.”
But in his next sentence, Vance began mocking former President Joe Biden, who is also expected to be in attendance and whose mental acuity the vice president has questioned.
“I’m also, as you guys can probably guess, I’m really looking forward to hanging out with Joe Biden. I’m sure that we’ll have many, many intense intellectual conversations,” Vance said.
Democrats’ campaign chief knocks GOP midterm convention — 2:21 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, the chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said her party is making its case to voters “district by district all across the country where it matters.”
In an interview with The Associated Press, she dismissed any notion that Democrats were missing an opportunity in not hosting a national event of their own.
“I don’t know what they’re doing,” she said of the GOP event. “They don’t have a message, they have nothing to say. So I think that will be even more clear next week.”
Vance says Driscoll and Hegseth are both his friends — 2:19 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The vice president sidestepped a question about Dan Driscoll’s exit from his role as U.S. Army secretary after reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
“Dan is obviously a very good friend of mine. I think he was a great secretary of the Army. Pete is also a very good friend of mine,” Vance said.
He then launched into a defense of the way Hegseth has run the department and changed the culture.
Vice President Vance says US got 15 million barrels of oil through Strait of Hormuz, lower than figures cited by Trump — 2:18 p.m.
By the Associated Press
JD Vance said the U.S. is finding ways to escort oil tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz and protect them from Iranian fire, but the administration can given conflicting figures on how much oil is involved.
“We got about 15 million barrels out of the Strait of Hormuz just yesterday,” Vance said at the White House briefing, saying that the operation occurred even though the Iranians continue to shoot at tankers.
That 15 million figure is meaningful, but it’s lower than the 18 million barrels that Trump posted on social media earlier in the day.
In a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said 17 million barrels were carried through the strait on Monday with assistance from the U.S. Navy.
Vance gives White House media briefing, but makes clear he’s not the new press secretary — 2:14 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Press secretary Karoline Leavitt has left the White House and Trump has yet to name a replacement. So the vice president stepped in Thursday to brief the media.
“Are we talking to you as the vice president or the press secretary,” Fox News White House reporter Peter Doocy asked Vance.
Vance referred to a meme about the many extra jobs Trump has given Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“I’m not Marco,” Vance joked. “I’ve not yet accepted any additional jobs.”
He said Trump wished him well while sparring with reporters, but warned if he did too well he might get the job full time.
“So I’ve got to screw up a little bit because I’m busy enough as it is,” he said. “But I’m very much up here as the vice president.”
Trump administration ratchets up its fight to get more oil flowing from California — 1:25 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The Trump administration is ratcheting up its fight to get more crude flowing through California and reverse the state’s efforts to move away from fossil fuels.
Its latest salvo is a federal review of California’s coastal management program, which is run largely by a state commission that has had a powerful role for decades in shaping development along the coast. Environmental advocates fear federal officials could use the review to strip the California Coastal Commission of its ability to have a say in projects involving federal agencies that affect the state’s rugged coastal bluffs, pristine beaches and world-class surfing spots.
The administration, citing a need for energy security and job creation, has already announced plans for new offshore oil leases in California as well as Florida, where the federal government has not allowed drilling since 1995 because of concerns about oil spills in the Gulf of Mexico.
Representative Hakeem Jeffries says he had ‘productive, forward-looking’ talk with wayward Democrat — 1:07 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The Democratic leader praised Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, the conservative Blue Dog Democrat who bucked her party this week on a procedural vote, as a lawmaker who is “fighting hard for her district.” It’s a region Trump carried.
“We value every single member in our caucus — progressives, new Dems and Blue Dogs,” Jeffries said. He said they spoke about moving forward on shared priorities.
“The entirety of the House Democratic caucus understands what the stakes are in terms of defeating MAGA extremism in November and then, as Democrats, getting off to a fast start in January,” he said.
The federal charges follow the officer’s release from jail last week — 12:26 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Christian Castro was released after Texas’ governor refused to immediately sign an extradition warrant to hand him over to Minnesota authorities, who have charged him separately with assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.
Federal authorities had initially accused Sosa-Celis and another man of beating an officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel during the confrontation. But federal prosecutors dropped charges against the men after video evidence showed the officers may have lied about the encounter, and officials opened an investigation.
AP Source: ICE officer charged with lying to investigators in the shooting of Venezuelan man — 12:24 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Federal prosecutors have charged a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with lying to investigators about the events leading up to the shooting of a Venezuelan man during the Minneapolis immigration crackdown earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
The person was not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke on condition of anonymity. The person said Christian Castro, the officer who authorities say shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg in January, has been charged with making false statements to federal investigators.
Trump hails Markey win, ‘I couldn’t stand Moulton’ — 12:09 p.m.
By Sam Brodey, Globe Staff
President Trump was following Massachusetts’ US Senate primary — and apparently, he’s happy with the result.
Speaking at a White House dinner for Republican candidates Wednesday night, Trump hailed what he called Senator Ed Markey’s 30-point “landslide” win over US Representative Seth Moulton in Tuesday’s primary election.
“I’m glad Markey won over Moulton,” Trump said. “I couldn’t stand Moulton. I really couldn’t. I mean, Markey, I wouldn’t say, loves Trump, but Moulton was so bad.”
It’s unclear exactly why Trump feels so strongly about Moulton. During the primary campaign, both Markey and Moulton ran as fierce Trump opponents, even jockeying to claim they would be tougher on the president than their opponent.
But Moulton previously was on Trump’s radar: after all, the Salem Democrat wanted to challenge him in 2020 for the presidency. Like many other Democrats who ran in that primary, Moulton campaigned as someone who could protect American democracy from the threat posed by Trump.
US House drops two weeks from its September schedule — 11:57 a.m.
By the Associated Press
House Republican leaders announced Thursday that they’re cutting their schedule short as they campaign to keep their majority in midterm elections.
House lawmakers who returned to Washington from their five-week August recess this week will now be in session only one additional week ahead of the November election, the week of Sept. 14. Members will then head back to their districts to campaign.
The Senate has been out of session since Aug. 8 and will return Sept. 14 for a three-week session ahead of the election.
Trump claims the US has ‘virtually unlimited’ munition stockpiles — 11:45 a.m.
By the Associated Press
In a Truth Social post, the president insisted the U.S. has “virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition,” for its war against Iran.
Trump added, “In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen.”
Earlier this week, Trump in an exchange with reporters suggested the U.S. could find creative ways to deal with munition shortages if necessary.
“But we can always take from other sources,” Trump told reporters Monday. “But I don’t think we’re going to need it because nobody’s going to mess with us. Nobody.”
The Associated Press reported last week, citing a U.S. defense official in Europe and a NATO official, that the U.S. military is experiencing a “beyond critical” shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe that’s largely driven by Trump’s war with Iran.
Trump administration pushes to remove tax exemption for private colleges with DEI policies — 11:43 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The administration is proposing a new rule that would strip private schools and colleges of their tax-exempt status if they provide targeted help to students based on their race, a significant escalation in the White House’s campaign to eradicate diversity programs directed at Black, Hispanic and other minority students.
The Treasury Department proposed the change Thursday in a new regulation that, if made final, would kick in after May 2027. The rule is broadly aimed at ending any policies or programs that help students because of their race, and it specifically says such benefits in admissions, scholarships and facilities “would be incompatible” with the rule.
It’s the latest attempt by the Trump administration to pressure schools and colleges to weed out diversity, equity and inclusion policies that had become common before Trump returned to the White House with a promise to end them. Trump officials have used Civil Rights-era laws to unwind the policies, saying they discriminate against white and Asian American students.
Venezuelans’ pride is bruised by deal to give US one-fifth of their oil reserves — 10:45 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Nothing has shaped what it means to be Venezuelan today more than oil.
For more than 100 years, in good times and bad, Venezuelans’ identity has been built around the belief that their country’s bountiful oil resources belong to the people, not a government or a company.
This belief, and a troubled nation’s pride, took a bruising last week when acting President Delcy Rodríguez agreed to give the United States control of roughly one-fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves — the largest in the world.
While the deal could eventually generate billions of dollars for an oil industry and economy wrecked by years of mismanagement, many Venezuelans see it as a surrender. Some say they’re not surprised; they believe gaining control of Venezuelan oil was the ultimate objective when President Trump ordered U.S. forces to capture then-President Nicolás Maduro at the beginning of the year, leaving Rodríguez in charge.
Trump administration ratchets up its fight to get more oil flowing from California — 10:22 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Its latest salvo is a federal review of California’s coastal management program, which is run largely by a state commission that’s had a powerful role for decades in shaping development along the coast. Environmental advocates fear federal officials could use the review to strip the California Coastal Commission of its ability to have a say in projects involving federal agencies that affect the state’s rugged coastal bluffs, pristine beaches and world-class surfing spots.
The administration, citing a need for energy security and job creation, has already announced plans for new offshore oil leases in California as well as Florida, where the federal government hasn’t allowed drilling since 1995 because of concerns about oil spills in the Gulf of Mexico.
Trump officials also helped a Texas firm jump-start an old pipeline system that had been idled since its 2015 rupture caused one of California’s worst oil spills, blackening beaches for 150 miles (240 kilometers) from Santa Barbara to Los Angeles and polluting habitat for endangered whales and sea turtles.
Democrats are promising a big agenda. Their unity is already being tested. — 9:30 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Beginning on Day One, House Democrats plan to “hold the crooks accountable.”
That’s the promise House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has made, previewing an ambitious agenda with oversight of President Trump’s administration and legislation to address the high costs of living, if Democrats seize majority control from Republicans in the midterm elections.
But first, the Democratic leaders have to ensure they can keep their own politically diverse — and sometimes rebellious — big-tent caucus in line, which was tested this week. Two go-their-own-way Democrats bucked the party on a routine procedural vote, angering colleagues and raising a red flag about potential party divisions to come.
“His greatest challenge will be governing,” Ashley Etienne, a former top aide to Nancy Pelosi during her historic tenure as House speaker, said of Jeffries.
US trade deficit widens despite Trump’s tariffs — 9:22 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The US trade deficit widened to $88.6 billion in July, up 24% from June and the highest since March 2025 when Trump was just beginning to ramp up import taxes to protect American industry from foreign competition. An investment boom in artificial intelligence is drawing in imports of computers and computer and telecommunications equipment.
Overall, US imports rose 2.8% in July and exports dropped 2.1%.
Still, the January-July deficit — the gap between what the US buys from and what it sells to other countries — is down nearly 30% from a year earlier.
Billionaire investor Leon Black sues House committee over Epstein investigation — 9:16 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Black refused to appear for a sworn deposition before Congress on Thursday and instead sued the House Oversight Committee, asking a federal court to block subpoenas issued as part of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein.
The House Oversight Committee served Black with two subpoenas following a closed-door interview in June after lawmakers said he refused to answer questions about nondisclosure agreements.
Black’s lawsuit argues the subpoenas exceed the committee’s authority by seeking private information.
“The Committee is on a fishing expedition that oversteps its authority and completely ignores its responsibility,” Black’s attorney, Susan Estrich, said in a statement.
Unemployment claims tick up to 206,000 but remain at historically low levels — 8:54 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The Labor Department reported Thursday filings for benefits ticked up to 206,000 last week from a revised 204,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, rose modestly to 207,250 last week.
Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. For the past year, claims have mostly stayed within a historically low range of 200,000 to 230,000 a week.
Companies, remembering the worker shortages that followed the end of COVID-19 lockups, are still reluctant to let go of staff. The unemployment rate is low at 4.1%.
Trump’s plan for a fence at Lafayette Park near White House gets review by federal panel — 8:35 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The latest pieces of President Trump’s wide-ranging Washington makeover are set for an airing Thursday in front of a federal panel that already has blessed other big-ticket plans from the designer-in-chief.
The National Capital Planning Commission, which this spring approved Trump’s White House ballroom proposal after he razed the Executive Mansion’s East Wing without authorization, will discuss a proposed fence around Lafayette Park in front of the White House.
The panel also will review a proposed underground security screening center for White House visitors. It’s the first time the commission will take up either idea, and votes aren’t expected. But the commission and the separate US Commission of Fine Arts thus far have not been an obstacle for Trump’s plans for the capital.
Trump factchecks his own commerce secretary on Iran war deaths — 7:41 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The president took the unusual step of correcting a misleading statement by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who had said in an interview that no US forces had died in the Iran war.
“Sec. Lutnick had Venezuela on his mind when he said nobody was killed,” Trump posted on social media. “18 people were killed in Iran!”
Lutnick had said in a Wednesday CNBC interview that no Americans had died in the conflict that began at the end of February. But Lutnick in his remarks was specifically talking about the Iran war, which he called “an economic chokeout.”
EPA proposal could leave the public in the dark on data center plans — 7:22 a.m.
By the Associated Press
A plan by the Environmental Protection Agency could make it harder for the public to learn about and comment on proposed AI data centers that have sparked backlash in communities across the United States and transformed the midterm election landscape.
The EPA proposal would eliminate a federal requirement that states notify the public and seek comment before issuing air pollution permits for data centers and other industrial facilities. States could still offer opportunities for public comment, but the EPA would no longer mandate them as a condition for states to grant permits.
Critics say the move could thwart local residents from learning about proposed data centers or making their voices heard before projects are approved and construction begins. The move comes during a widespread backlash as tech giants build hundreds of massive server warehouses to fuel artificial intelligence and cloud computing.
Lawmakers ask Army to explain why it told a military unit to stop specializing in drone warfare — 7:03 a.m.
By the Associated Press
A bipartisan group of US lawmakers is pressing the Army to explain why it told a unit based in Europe to stop specializing in drone warfare, an order that comes as the world’s battlefields rapidly evolve and military tactics increasingly rely on uncrewed systems to fight.
The 173rd Airborne Brigade was building its own drones and practicing the kind of warfare that Ukraine has pioneered against Russia and that Iran has fought against the US — warfare that has killed and wounded American troops. The brigade of 600 soldiers was set up in November to be deployed anywhere that drones were needed.
“We have deep concerns that eliminating this specialized drone unit will limit our ability to learn from allies, particularly the Ukrainian Armed Forces, and hinder our efforts to modernize drone warfare at the speed necessary to compete on the modern battlefield,” the lawmakers said in a letter shared with The Associated Press.
It requests a briefing from the Army to explain its decision and was sent Tuesday to departing Army Secretary Dan Driscoll and Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army’s acting chief of staff.
Homeland Security says August immigration arrests set new record — 6:58 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The Trump administration reports that the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested 50,925 people in August 2026.
The Department of Homeland Security says it’s the third consecutive monthly record. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin credited Trump for an aggressive mass deportation program.
“ICE is working around the clock every day to arrest and deport illegal aliens from American communities,” the secretary said. “If you are in the country illegally, LEAVE NOW. If not, we will find you, arrest you, and deport you.”
A recent AP-NORC poll found that just 39% of US adults approve of his performance on immigration, a decline from 49% at the beginning of his second term. The poll also found that about half of US adults say Trump has “gone too far” on deporting immigrants living in the U.S. illegally.
Federal judge considers whether to extend ban against US Postal Service mail voting changes — 6:57 a.m.
By the Associated Press
A federal judge in Boston will hear arguments Thursday on whether to extend her prohibition against the US Postal Service requiring states to use a new mail balloting system for the midterms as part of an executive order by President Trump.
The hearing in the closely watched case comes the day before the first state begins sending mail ballots to voters.
US District Court Judge Indira Talwani is considering whether to order a preliminary injunction that would bar the Postal Service from requiring the new system to be used for the midterms. Last week, she imposed a 14-day temporary restraining order to keep it from being used. That order expires next week as more states begin sending out mail ballots.
Trump promises to campaign for Republicans and says they have a winning midterm message — 6:49 a.m.
By the Associated Press
President Trump on Wednesday urged Republican lawmakers facing tough reelection campaigns to run on his record in the White House despite his sagging popularity, and he pledged to campaign in all of the roughly three dozen contests that are likely to determine control of Congress.
Voters’ dim views of the economy and the war in Iran have put Republicans in a tough spot as the midterm election season enters its final stretch. But during a dinner in the Rose Garden, one of the spaces he has controversially renovated since returning to office last year, the president told his party’s most vulnerable lawmakers that they had a triumphant story to tell voters.
“All you have to do is talk about it, and you’re going to win and you’re going to win big,” Trump said a week before the party gathers in Dallas for an unusual midterm convention.
Trump puts tariffs of up to 100% on foreign-made drones — 12:30 a.m.
By the New York Times
A 100% tariff applies to drones that weigh more than 55 pounds or use thermal imaging. Those drones, the vast majority of which are made in China, have become essential for many law enforcement officials, as they’re used to track wildfires and find lost people. Smaller drones have a tariff of 25%.
President Donald Trump, whose two eldest sons have ties to the U.S. drone industry, announced the levies last month after a Commerce Department investigation deemed reliance on foreign drones and components a national security threat.
The Trump administration argued that the United States must be weaned off its reliance on China for drone technology. It is estimated that a single Chinese company -- Shenzhen-based DJI -- manufactures more than 70% of the world’s commercial drones.
Judge blocks Trump’s new bid to curb birthright citizenship — 12:00 a.m.
By the Associated Press
A federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to limit birthright citizenship, granting a preliminary injunction against an executive order that the administration said would target “birth tourism.”
U.S. District Judge Deborah L. Boardman in Maryland on Wednesday issued the injunction until a class-action lawsuit brought by immigrant families and advocacy groups is resolved.
“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” Boardman, appointed by President Joe Biden, wrote in Wednesday’s ruling.
Birthright citizenship is guaranteed under current law for anyone who is born on U.S. soil, with a few exceptions. The law stretches back to 1868, when the 14th Amendment was ratified in the aftermath of the Civil War.

sources.news_title: ICE Officer Accused of Lying to Investigators About Minnesota Shooting
sources.text:
Christian Castro, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who shot a fleeing man in Minneapolis in January, has been indicted by a federal grand jury for making false statements about the incident, according to a source familiar with the case.
The case, which is still under seal according to the source, who is not authorized to speak publicly about it, adds more scrutiny to the militarized tactics adopted by federal immigration agents during the Trump administration’s Operation Metro Surge, which flooded Minnesota with roving deportation patrols earlier this year.
The Justice Department’s decision to charge Castro comes as Minnesota was essentially blocked from prosecuting him with four counts of second-degree assault at the state level. The federal charge was first reported by The Associated Press.
On Jan. 14, Castro chased a Venezuelan man, Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, as he fled into a Minneapolis home, which was occupied at the time, and shot him. Sosa-Celis was initially charged with assaulting an officer, but the case was dropped when prosecutors were presented evidence that contradicted Castro’s claims that he fired his service weapon after being attacked.
Trending
Castro, 52, was arrested in May by Texas Rangers, who were flanked by Minnesota investigators. Castro was kept in a Cameron County jail for the statutory maximum of 90 days — but he was released last week when Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign extradition papers and successfully fought off Minnesota’s legal challenge trying to force his hand.
While the federal charges break what has been until now an impasse to hold Castro accountable for overly aggressive behavior while on duty, the decision is still sure to draw criticism. According to ProPublica, these new criminal charges are significantly pared down from what federal prosecutors initially planned: deprivation of rights under color of law.
ProPublica cited an email from the lead federal prosecutor, Matthew Evans, to Sosa-Celis’ lawyers on the eve of the indictment that informed the victim about his dashed efforts to make a stronger case. In that email, quoted by ProPublica, Evans wrote that “this is being directed by the Main Justice and the US Attorney,” adding that “I objected in the strongest possible terms and fought it as hard as I could. It wasn’t enough.”
Hennepin County still has an active warrant for his arrest, although the state investigation could take a backseat to the new federal case.
According to the state complaint, the Minneapolis Police Department received a call from a 911 dispatcher on Jan. 14 at 6:43 p.m. saying that ICE agents were chasing after a man driving a Ford Focus. Two minutes later, local police officers remotely took control of a city camera at a nearby intersection allowing them to monitor what happened next.
At 6:47, Sosa-Celis is seen holding a snow shovel as he steps onto the home’s front lawn. A minute later, the man being chased by ICE agents drives up to the house, gets out of the car and flees, the complaint says. Video shows Castro drive up then chase the man on foot. Sosa-Celis drops the snow shovel as the two get closer.
During a struggle with the ICE agent, the man falls. Sosa-Celis helps him up and the two run inside the house. the complaint says. Three seconds later, Castro can be seen raising his gun and firing a single shot into the house — which was also captured by the city’s nearby “ShotSpotter” acoustic gunshot-detection system.
Sosa-Celis was shot in the right leg, the complaint says. He and two others were arrested by the Department of Homeland Security, which referred to them as “criminal illegal aliens” who “were let into our country by the Biden administration.”
According to the state complaint, another ICE agent later told state investigators and FBI agents that Castro had reported someone swung a broom swung at him and that he was hit twice by a shovel.
In a statement the next day, then-Homeland Security Kristi Noem said that “what we saw last night in Minneapolis was an attempted murder of federal law enforcement. Our officer was ambushed and attacked by three individuals who beat him with snow shovels and the handles of brooms. Fearing for his life, the officer fired a defensive shot.”
However, Minnesota state investigators determined that Castro’s description was a fabrication and charged him with three felony counts of second-degree assault with a dangerous weapon and one misdemeanor count of falsely reporting a crime.
This story has been updated with original reporting from NOTUS.

sources.news_title: AP Source: Feds charge ICE officer with lying to investigators in Minneapolis shooting
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — Federal prosecutors have charged a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with lying to investigators about the events leading up to the shooting of a Venezuelan man during the Minneapolis immigration crackdown earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
Christian Castro, the officer who authorities say shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg in January, has been charged with making false statements to federal investigators, according to the person, who was not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The federal charges, which remain under seal, follow Castro’s release from jail last week after Texas’ governor refused to immediately sign an extradition warrant to hand him over to Minnesota authorities, who have charged him separately with assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.
Federal authorities had initially accused Sosa-Celis and another man of beating an officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel during the confrontation. But federal prosecutors dropped charges against the men after video evidence showed the officers may have lied about the encounter, and officials opened an investigation.
Charges stem from nonfatal shooting during Operation Metro Surge
Castro is the first federal immigration officer to be prosecuted by the Trump administration related to actions taken during the massive Operation Metro Surge in the Twin Cities that began in January 2026. No attorney is listed for Castro in the case brought by Minnesota and it was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer to speak on his behalf.
Thousands of officers were sent to the Minneapolis and St. Paul area by the Department of Homeland Security in what was its largest immigration enforcement operation ever. The shooting deaths of U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers drew condemnation and raised questions over officers’ conduct, prompting changes to the operation.
Earlier this week, a federal prosecutor working on the case told lawyers for Sosa-Celis and other victims that Justice Department officials blocked the prosecutor’s push to bring a more serious civil rights charge against the officer for the shooting, ProPublica reported on Wednesday.
But the person familiar with the investigation disputed the prosecutor’s characterization, saying the civil rights probe is continuing and there has been no final decision on whether to bring additional charges. The prosecutor, Matthew Evans, has been fired and is under investigation for alleged obstruction of a grand jury probe, the person said.
An automatic email response from Evans’ Justice Department account said he was on leave. Other attempts to reach him were not immediately successful.
An attorney for Sosa-Celis said the Justice Department has “grossly undercharged this case,” adding that Castro’s statements were made to “cover up the fact that he shot my client through the door of an occupied house without a self-defense justification.”
“Mr. Sosa Celis wants Mr. Castro to be held fully accountable for his crimes,” said the attorney, Robin Wolpert. The American Liberties Union of Minnesota said Thursday that Sosa-Celis also plans to seek damages from the federal government.
Castro is also facing charges from Minnesota authorities
Castro was initially arrested in May in the Minnesota case, and he was held in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico, while Minnesota officials sought his extradition. But Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to immediately sign off, citing continuing investigations of fraud in government social service programs in Minnesota, which Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.
Minnesota officials had sought to stop the sheriff in Cameron County, Texas, from releasing Castro, out of fear that he would flee to Mexico. According to a lawsuit filed by Minnesota, Castro had a conversation with a woman, while he was incarcerated, where he spoke about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico after his release.
But Castro was released a week ago after a federal judge refused to order Texas to extradite him.
The Department of Homeland Security previously called Minnesota’s prosecution of Castro “unlawful and nothing more than a political stunt,” saying only federal authorities have jurisdiction in the case.
Castro was placed on leave during the federal probe
Castro was suspended from ICE without pay in February while federal authorities conducted the investigation.
“The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct,” ICE’s acting director at the time, Todd Lyons, said then. “Violations of this sacred sworn oath will not be tolerated. ICE remains fully committed to transparency, accountability, and the fair enforcement of our nation’s immigration laws.”
Minnesota officials alleged that Castro, 52, fired through the front door of a home and shot Sosa-Celis in the thigh.
Castro and another officer had chased a different man, Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna, to the Minneapolis apartment duplex where he and Sosa-Celis lived. Minnesota prosecutors said the officer then falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.
Attorneys for Sosa-Celis and Aljorna didn’t immediately respond to emails Thursday from the AP.
Gonzalez reported from McAllen, Texas.

sources.news_title: For the First Time, Federal Prosecutors Charge One of Their Own ICE Agents with a Felony
sources.text:
For the First Time, Federal Prosecutors Charge One of Their Own ICE Agents with a Felony
But with that said, federal prosecutors are still letting ICE agent Christian Castro off easy.
Photo: Getty Images, Stephen Maturen Splinter ICE
Well, it’s a milestone, even if it is a rather tepid one: For the first time in the second Trump administration, criminal charges have been brought against a federal agent of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) by a member of Trump’s own Justice Department–federal charges against a fed.
That lucky ICE agent is 52-year-old Christian Castro, who allegedly shot and wounded Venezuelan native Julio Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis in January while firing through a closed door in what the Department of Homeland Security immediately claimed were “defensive” shots. Castro is accused by federal prosecutors on charges of making false statements (a class D felony) for lying about the circumstances of the shooting, spinning a story about having been attacked by multiple people armed with shovels and broomsticks, before emerging video evidence eventually contradicted his entire account. Subsequently, even acting ICE Director Todd Lyons was forced to admit, before Congress, that ICE agents in the case had been demonstrably lying. On a national level, the case generated significantly fewer headlines than the ICE and CBP shooting deaths of American citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti that bookended it, both of which may still result in charges of their own.
With all that said, even though Donald Trump’s Justice Department has now charged Castro with a crime, they’ve actually gone far out of their way to make the actual charges significantly less severe than originally anticipated. According to none other than the federal prosecutor handling the case, assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Evans, federal prosecutors in Minnesota had been preparing to charge Castro with more serious “deprivation of rights under color of law,” civil rights charges that would have carried significantly higher penalties and a threat of longer jail time. Unnamed DOJ leaders stepped in, according to Evans, to insist that those charges be reduced to only the one of making false statements. Evans told lawyers for Sosa-Celis as much in an email reviewed by ProPublica, rather shockingly blaming his superiors for pushing for lesser charges. As Evans reportedly put it in that email: “This is being directed by the Main Justice and the US attorney. I objected in the strongest possible terms and fought it as hard as I could. It wasn’t enough. It has been an honor and a privilege to try to get justice for your clients.”
DO NOT CELEBRATE THE MEEK FEDERAL CHARGES AGAINST ICE AGENT CHRISTIAN CASTRO. They are a mockery of justice. Prosecutors were all set to charge Castro with a much more serious criminal civil rights violation, but Trump stooges at Main Justice refused to sign off. www.propublica.org/article/doj-…
— Dan Froomkin/Press Watch/Heads Up News (@froomkin.bsky.social) 2:53 PM · Sep 3, 2026
Which is all to say, even when the Trump DOJ does get around to finally charging one of its ICE agents with a crime, they’re pretty clearly still trying to protect the guy from greater degree of scrutiny. They’re merely charging Castro with how he wronged the Trump administration (by lying), rather than charging him with how he wronged Julio Sosa-Celis. Regardless, Castro is still facing a handful of charges from Minnesota’s Hennepin County Attorney’s Office as well, including four counts of second-degree assault with a dangerous weapon, and one count of falsely reporting a crime. There should be a good number of felonies to go around, here.
Provided, that is, Christian Castro can actually be sent to Minnesota to stand trial. Just last week, we wrote about the extradition battle that was raging over the same ICE agent, with an obstinate state of Texas (Castro’s home) and Gov. Greg Abbott (R) personally stepping in to take what should have been a routine extradition of an indicted person and turn it into a culture war proxy battle. Abbott’s office, citing completely random, unrelated bullshit—like investigations of fraud in the state of Minnesota’s social services—dragged its feet for more than three months after apprehending Castro, in a seeming effort to allow that 90-day extradition incarceration limit to expire and free Castro. He walked out the doors of a Texas jail on Aug. 27, after a Trump-appointed federal judge sided with the state of Texas and ruled that Abbott was under no pressure to decide whether to extradite Castro.
All the more absurd: Minnesota had brought its lawsuit attempting to compel Abbott to extradite Castro specifically because Minnesota prosecutors say they fear that Castro will attempt to flee to Mexico to avoid prosecution. According to their court filings, Castro had been having “monitored conversations” while in custody with “a woman south of the border,” and had specifically been heard literally mentioning plans “about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released.” His current whereabouts? Unknown, as far as we can tell. Surely, ICE itself will be stepping in at any moment now to collar one of their rogue agents and bring him to face not just state, but federal charges?
Christian Castro, the ICE agent who shot a man that fled into a home in Minneapolis, had a restraining order filed against him by his wife back in Texas.
And from jail he’s been calling a girlfriend in Mexico — where he plans to go.
New reporting in @notus.com:
www.notus.org/courts/minne…
— Jose Pagliery (@josepagliery.bsky.social) 6:35 PM · Aug 25, 2026
Ironically, federal prosecutors have more power in getting a defendant extradited from one state to another, and with federal charges they would not need to wait for Greg Abbott to sign off on the transfer–and presumably he would do so, because saying no in this case wouldn’t be just opposing the evil, corrupt state of Minnesota, but saying no to Papa Trump’s DOJ. But because the federal prosecutors waited to finally indict Castro until after he had already been released from custody in Texas, they can’t simply scoop him up from the jail where he was being held for those 90 days.
We’re now more or less back to square one: Castro may be a fugitive, or he may be negotiating his surrender, or he may be in custody and it simply hasn’t been announced anywhere.
